_note: Written with AI assistance (Claude Code). Generated by scripts/build-investigations.mjs from docs/research/psi_investigations.json; never edit by hand. Sorted by PSI accession number, not by relevance.
relevance_note: Relevance scores (whole numbers 1 to 5, one per crew setting) are the Still Air team's judgment, not NASA's: they follow the rubric in docs/research/psi_investigations_catalog.md, were assigned with AI assistance, and have not been reviewed by a subject-matter expert. Key findings are quoted from the source named next to each one.

investigations.full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
investigations.fire_safety_theme: fundamental (soot and radiative extinction; stated spacecraft fire-safety implications)

years.operations: ISS test days 2019 (normal flames, test IDs 19xxx) and 2021 (inverse flames, 21xxx); ISS Increments 59-60 and 66

investigations.hardware: ACME chamber insert; porous spherical burners (6.35-12.7 mm dia family); thermocouple rakes
investigations.fuel_sample: Gaseous ethylene (and propane, one day) with N2 dilution; normal (fuel out) and inverse (oxidizer out) spherical diffusion flames

atmosphere.o2: Normal flames ambient XO2 0.198-0.40; inverse flames burner-supply XO2 0.21-0.85

investigations.flow: Quiescent ambient; burner total flow 0.6-12.2 mg/s
investigations.pi: Richard Axelbaum (Washington University in St. Louis); Co-Is Peter Sunderland (UMD), David Urban (GRC)
investigations.key_finding: Across ambient O2 0.2-0.38, fuel fraction 0.13-1 and 0.6-12.2 mg/s, all ethylene spherical flames reached radiative extinction at a critical temperature of 1130 K (fuel mass flux 0.2 g/m2-s normal; O2 mass flux 0.68 g/m2-s inverse).
investigations.key_finding_source: Irace et al. 2023 abstract reproduced in ACME/Flame Design Final Report (PSI-10)

key_papers.citation: Irace P.H., Waddell K.A., Constales D., Sunderland P.B., Axelbaum R.L., et al. (2023). Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 39.

Irace P.H., Lee H.J., Waddell K., Tan L., Stocker D.P., Sunderland P.B., et al. (2021). Observations of long duration microgravity spherical diffusion flames aboard the International Space Station. Combustion and Flame 229.

spacecraft_cabin.why: A single extinction temperature (1130 K) is a usable model input for cabin fire predictions; gaseous fuel, not materials.

lunar_base.why: Tests up to 40% ambient O2 overlap the lunar atmosphere range; still a burner, not a material.

notes_unverified: Pressure ranges are from PSI table 'pmean' columns.

investigations.full_name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.fire_safety_theme: prevention (material flammability in quiescent, elevated-O2 atmospheres)

years.operations: ISS test days Feb 2019 - Jan 2021 (18 rows in PSI table)

investigations.hardware: ACME chamber insert in CIR; flat porous burners 25 mm and 50 mm dia with 2 heat-flux gauges each
investigations.fuel_sample: Gaseous emulator: C2H4 (50% and 100%, N2 balance) and CH4 fed through flat porous burners to emulate condensed fuels (PMMA, Nylon, alcohols); heat of combustion 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g

atmosphere.pressure: ~0.56 to 1 bar; NASA habitat atmospheres 14.7 psia/21%, 10.2 psia/26.5%, 8.2 psia/34%

investigations.flow: Quiescent (no forced ambient flow); fuel mass flux set by burner

psi_data.file_types: 1049 ZIP (2016.29 GB), 652 TXT, 383 CSV (1.109 GB), 199 MP4 (16.005 GB), 59 PDF (0.185 GB), 10 MDIPSUG, 5 XLSX, 2 DOCX, 1 ZIIP (1.973 GB), 1 NEXT

investigations.pi: James Quintiere (University of Maryland); Co-I John de Ris; Project Scientists Peter Sunderland (UMD), Dennis Stocker (NASA GRC)
investigations.key_finding: In still microgravity air, steady flames over an emulated 25 mm flat material occurred at nominal O2 of ~26% and above (including the NASA 10.2 psia/26.5% and 8.2 psia/34% atmospheres), whereas 21% O2 flames self-extinguished; an emulated material like PMMA (hc~24 kJ/g, L~3 kJ/g) burned steadily at 26.5%/10.2 psia. Radiative loss fraction reached ~60% vs ~30% in 1 g. 59 ignited tests.
investigations.key_finding_source: ACME/BRE Final Report 2022 (PSI-20) 'Surprises' and results sections; Dehghani et al. 2021 abstract (Semantic Scholar)

key_papers.citation: Dehghani P., Sunderland P.B., Quintiere J.G., deRis J.L. (2021). Burning in microgravity: Experimental results and analysis. Combustion and Flame 228.
Dehghani P., de Ris J.L., Quintiere J.G. (2023). Demonstrating steady burning for small flat materials in microgravity in a quiescent ambient. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 39.

spacecraft_cabin.why: Shows that turning off ventilation (a standard spacecraft fire response) may not extinguish fires in enriched O2; cabin is normally 21%.

iss.why: ISS uses 21% O2 where these flames self-extinguished, so the risk is lower but the 'fans-off' assumption is tested.

lunar_base.why: Only PSI dataset run at the planned exploration atmospheres (26.5%/10.2 psia, 34%/8.2 psia) that match the >=30% O2 lunar base.

mars_base.why: Same exploration atmospheres; micro-g bound for 0.38 g.

pressurized_rover.why: Rovers are expected to use the same high-O2/low-pressure atmosphere; still-air burning applies to a small cabin with fans off.

notes_unverified: Mars-base atmosphere is not specified in the challenge text; scoring assumes it resembles the lunar exploration atmosphere.

investigations.key_finding: In microgravity the voltage-current curve has a distinct peak ion current at the most compact flame instead of the 1-g saturation plateau; very weak flames that would quench were stabilized by small fields. investigations.pi: No single PI in PSI record; Co-Is: Paul Ferkul (NASA GRC), Carlos Fernandez-Pello (UC Berkeley), Fletcher Miller (SDSU), James T'ien (Case Western), Subrata Bhattacharjee (SDSU); Sandra Olson (NASA GRC) is lead author of the Summary Report
investigations.key_finding: Over PMMA cylinders, microgravity flame spread was sustained down to 17% O2 versus 18% in normal gravity, and spread rate first rose then fell as opposed flow increased from 0.4 to 8 cm/s (not seen on Earth). Across BASS-II, most tests released well under 100 W and burned fuel-rich (global equivalence ratio ~1.3).

key_papers.citation: Link S., Huang X., Fernandez-Pello C., Olson S., Ferkul P. (2018). The Effect of Gravity on Flame Spread over PMMA Cylinders. Scientific Reports 8.
Olson S.L., Ferkul P.V. (2017). Microgravity flammability boundary for PMMA rods in axial stagnation flow: Experimental results and energy balance analyses. Combustion and Flame 180.

spacecraft_cabin.why: Real cabin materials (PMMA, cotton-fiberglass, Nomex) at ventilation-scale flows (0-53 cm/s) give low-g flammability limits that the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 test cannot.

iss.why: Run in the ISS MSG at ISS cabin conditions; directly informs ISS material selection and fans-off procedures.

lunar_base.why: Strong micro-g end-member for bounding lunar gravity, but O2 never exceeded 22.2%, below the >=30% planned lunar atmosphere.

mars_base.why: Same as lunar: micro-g bound for 0.38 g, but no elevated-O2 or reduced-pressure tests.

pressurized_rover.why: Low-flow results matter in a small rover cabin, but rover atmospheres (high O2, low pressure) were not tested.

notes_unverified: Pressure is not in the PSI table; '~1 atm' is inferred from ISS cabin operation.
PSI 'Calibrated final O2' column contains a 40.4 value that looks like a data-entry error; not used.

investigations.key_finding: Limiting oxygen index for quasi-steady burning was 0.12 (methanol) and 0.15 (heptane) in O2/N2, rising to ~0.14 and ~0.17 when CO2 was added (simulated CO2 suppressant at 1 atm), and ~0.14/0.15 with helium. investigations.key_finding_source: Dietrich et al. 2014 abstract (OpenAlex)

key_papers.citation: Dietrich D.L., Nayagam V., Hicks M.C., Ferkul P.V., Dryer F.L., Farouk T., et al. (2014). Droplet Combustion Experiments Aboard the International Space Station. Microgravity Science and Technology 26.

investigations.fuel_sample: SIBAL fabric (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass), 40.6 cm wide x 94 cm long x 0.37 mm thick (concurrent); ~10 cm opposed-flow sample
investigations.flow: 20 cm/s forced air, concurrent and opposed

psi_data.file_types: 62 ZIP (12.179 GB), 6 PDF, 4 XLSX (0.065 GB), 3 DOCX, 1 CSV

investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC)
investigations.key_finding: Largest fire burned in space at the time: concurrent spread over the 40.6 x 94 cm fabric averaged 1.8 mm/s with an estimated flame power of 1200 +/- 300 W; burn lasted 420 s and consumed ~84 cm. Opposed-flow spread was 1.3 mm/s.
investigations.key_finding_source: Urban et al., ASGSR 2017 presentation, NTRS 20180005168 (Table 1 and Saffire-1 slide)

key_papers.citation: Urban D.L., Ferkul P., Olson S., Ruff G.A., Easton J., T'ien J.S., et al. (2019). Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale. Combustion and Flame 199.

Li C., Liao Y.-T.T., T'ien J.S., Urban D.L., Ferkul P., Olson S., et al. (2019). Transient flame growth and spread processes over a large solid fabric in concurrent low-speed flows in microgravity - Model versus experiment. Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 37.

spacecraft_cabin.why: A real fire inside a real spacecraft at realistic scale and ventilation speed (20 cm/s): the closest analogue to a cabin fire.

iss.why: Same scale and flow as ISS module ventilation; samples are spacecraft fabrics.

lunar_base.why: Fire growth at practical scale informs habitat design, but only ~21.5% O2 and micro-g.

mars_base.why: As lunar: scale data useful, gravity and atmosphere not matched.

pressurized_rover.why: Cygnus free volume is closer to a rover cabin than any other PSI test; fire power vs. small cabin volume is directly relevant.

notes_unverified: PSI investigation dates (2001-2008) do not match the 2016 flight; treat as a PSI metadata error.
Spread rates are from a NASA slide deck, not a peer-reviewed table.

investigations.full_name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II

years.operations: Launched OA-5 2016-10-17; burned 2016-11-21 in Cygnus (NTRS 20180005168)

investigations.hardware: Saffire module with nine-sample card
investigations.fuel_sample: Nine 5 cm x 29 cm samples: silicone (0.27, 0.61, 1.03 mm), SIBAL cotton-fiberglass 0.37 mm (x2), PMMA + Nomex, PMMA (shaped and 1 cm thick)
investigations.flow: 20 cm/s (one SIBAL test at 25 cm/s); concurrent and opposed

psi_data.file_types: 190 ZIP (16.678 GB), 11 XLSX (0.231 GB), 10 DOCX, 5 PDF, 1 CSV

investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC); Investigator Gary Ruff (NASA GRC)
investigations.key_finding: Silicone samples ignited but showed insignificant burning in microgravity at ~22.1% O2 and 20 cm/s, while the 0.27 mm silicone burned completely (accelerating) in the 1-g test; cotton-fiberglass spread at 2.1 mm/s (20 cm/s) and 2.6 mm/s (25 cm/s); average flame power ~200 +/- 50 W.
investigations.key_finding_source: NTRS 20180005168 Table 1 and slides; PSI-99 experimental table

key_papers.citation: Urban D.L., et al. (2019). Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale. Combustion and Flame 199.
Olson S.L., Urban D.L., Ruff G.A., Ferkul P.V., Toth B., Eigenbrod C., et al. (2019). Concurrent Flame Spread Over Two-Sided Thick PMMA Slabs in Microgravity. Fire Technology 56.

spacecraft_cabin.why: Directly tests whether materials passing/failing the 1-g screening test behave the same in a spacecraft.

iss.why: Materials and flow speed representative of ISS cabin.

lunar_base.why: Material-limit comparison is the key lunar question, but O2 ~22% only.

pressurized_rover.why: Material choice for a rover cabin; rover O2 levels not tested.

notes_unverified: PSI table column header '?-g' is a mis-encoded 'micro-g'.

investigations.full_name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III
investigations.fire_safety_theme: large-scale fire growth in a spacecraft

years.operations: Launched OA-7 2017-03-27 (NTRS deck) / burned 2017-06-04 in Cygnus

investigations.hardware: Saffire module, same design as Saffire-I
investigations.fuel_sample: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric 40.6 cm x 94 cm x 0.33-0.37 mm (concurrent) and ~10 cm opposed sample
investigations.flow: 25 cm/s per NASA ASGSR 2017 deck; PSI table says 30 cm/s (CONFLICT, see notes)

psi_data.file_types: 68 ZIP (35.115 GB), 7 PDF (0.012 GB), 6 XLSX (0.073 GB), 3 CSV, 3 DOCX

investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC)
investigations.key_finding: Concurrent spread over the large fabric was 2.3 mm/s (burn ~300-320 s), faster than Saffire-I's 1.8 mm/s at 20 cm/s; NASA notes flame speed scaled with air-flow velocity. Opposed spread was 0.98 mm/s.
investigations.key_finding_source: NTRS 20180005168 Table 1 and Saffire-I/III results slide

key_papers.citation: Urban D.L., et al. (2019). Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale. Combustion and Flame 199.

spacecraft_cabin.why: Repeat of the large spacecraft fire at higher flow shows how ventilation speeds up spread.

lunar_base.why: Ventilation/scale effects transfer; gravity and O2 do not match.

pressurized_rover.why: Shows fire growth vs. fan speed in an enclosed vehicle volume, directly useful for rover ventilation shutdown logic.

notes_unverified: Flow speed conflict: 25 cm/s (NASA 2017 deck) vs 30 cm/s (PSI experimental table, 2016 plan said 'close to 30 cm/s').
Burn duration 300 s (deck Table 1) vs 320 s (deck slide text).

investigations.full_name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

years.operations: ISS 2010-07-16 to 2010-09-09, 66 test points (final report)

investigations.hardware: SAME hardware with new M-pass instrument (replaced one Commercial Diagnostic Enclosure)
investigations.fuel_sample: Overheated Kapton, silicone, lampwick, Teflon, Pyrell intumescent foam (109 table rows)
investigations.flow: Inlet velocity 0, 1, 2, 8 and 8.1 cm/s (no-flow cases added)
investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC); Co-Is Zeng-guang Yuan (GRC), Jiann Yang and Thomas Cleary (NIST), George Mulholland (UMD)
investigations.key_finding: With no air flow, smoke particles were 2-3 times larger than at the nominal 8 cm/s flow (final report); averaged over materials, the diameter of average mass rose by a factor of 1.9 at no flow (Mulholland et al. 2015).
investigations.key_finding_source: SAME-R Final Report (PSI-101) conclusions; Mulholland et al. 2015 abstract (OpenAlex)

key_papers.citation: Mulholland G.W., Meyer M., Urban D.L., Ruff G.A., Yuan Z., Bryg V., et al. (2015). Pyrolysis Smoke Generated Under Low-Gravity Conditions. Aerosol Science and Technology 49.
Meyer M.E., et al. (2018). Evaluation of spacecraft smoke detector performance in the low-gravity environment. Fire Safety Journal 98.

spacecraft_cabin.why: No-flow smoke (e.g., overheating electronics in a closed rack) grows larger, changing which detector works.

iss.why: ISS racks and stagnant pockets are exactly the no-flow case.

lunar_base.why: Detector design transfers; partial-g settling not tested.

pressurized_rover.why: Stagnant, cramped rover compartments match the no-flow condition most closely.

investigations.full_name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.fire_safety_theme: detection (smoke particle size vs. detector type)

years.operations: ISS Increment 15, 2007-09-09 to 2007-10-05 (SAME-R final report)

investigations.hardware: SAME smoke generator (heated samples), aging chamber, thermal precipitator, Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures
investigations.fuel_sample: Overheated (pyrolyzed, not flaming) Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lampwick, dibutyl phthalate (8 samples)
investigations.flow: Air flow over sample 5 and 10 cm/s; aging 1-20 min
diagnostics: TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter (0th moment)
ionization chamber from residential smoke detector (1st moment)
investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC); Co-Is George Mulholland (UMD), Thomas Cleary and Jiann Yang (NIST)
investigations.key_finding: All materials produced large numbers of sub-micron (<1 micrometer) smoke particles that ionization detectors catch better; later analysis found ISS smoke particles varied in morphology and size but were not significantly different from 1-g equivalents.
investigations.key_finding_source: SAME Final Science Report (PSI-102) conclusions; Meyer et al. 2018 abstract/TLDR (Semantic Scholar)

key_papers.citation: Meyer M.E., Urban D.L., Mulholland G.W., Bryg V., Yuan Z.-G., Ruff G.A., et al. (2018). Evaluation of spacecraft smoke detector performance in the low-gravity environment. Fire Safety Journal 98.

spacecraft_cabin.why: Pre-fire overheat smoke from cabin materials is what cabin detectors must catch first.

iss.why: Evaluated the actual spacecraft smoke detectors under ISS conditions.

lunar_base.why: Detector design transfers, but partial-g settling and lunar dust nuisance sources are untested.

pressurized_rover.why: Early detection is critical in a small rover with little escape volume; same partial-g gap.

notes_unverified: The final report text says 'four materials' while the PSI table lists five; not resolved.

investigations.pi: David Urban (NASA GRC); Co-I Peter Sunderland (UMD)
